body: How should you prepare for a 5-minute talk?
options: Read your notes once silently
Memorise it word for word and never look up
Practise aloud a few times and time yourself
Skip practice so it sounds natural
explanation: Practising aloud shows where you stumble and whether you fit the time.

body: You feel nervous just before speaking. What helps most?
options: Speak very fast to finish quickly
Take a few slow breaths and focus on your first line
Keep apologising for being nervous
Avoid looking at anyone
explanation: Slow breathing calms the body, and a well-rehearsed opening gets you started.

body: Where should you look while speaking to a group?
options: Make eye contact with different people around the room
Only at your slides
At the floor
Above everyone's heads
explanation: Eye contact keeps the audience engaged and makes you look confident.

body: Which is a good way to open a talk?
options: 'Sorry, I am not well prepared'
Reading the title slide word for word
Going straight into technical detail
A short question, fact or story related to the topic
explanation: A strong opening catches attention and tells the audience why the topic matters.

body: How can you reduce filler words such as 'umm' and 'like'?
options: Speak faster
Replace them with 'basically'
Pause briefly instead of filling the silence
Never pause at all
explanation: A short pause sounds confident and gives you time to think.

body: How loud should you speak in a classroom without a microphone?
options: As softly as in a normal conversation
Loud enough for the last row to hear clearly
As loud as possible, close to shouting
Softly, to make people lean in
explanation: If the back row cannot hear you, your message is lost.

body: What is a good way to end a talk?
options: Summarise the key points and finish with a clear closing line
Just stop and walk off
Say 'That's it, I guess'
Introduce a new topic
explanation: A clear ending tells the audience what to remember.

body: What should your slides do during a talk?
options: Contain your full script
Be read aloud word for word
Use small text to fit everything
Support what you say with few words and clear visuals
explanation: The audience should listen to you, not read a wall of text.

body: What posture works best while speaking?
options: Lean on the table
Keep your hands in your pockets throughout
Stand upright with feet steady and hands relaxed
Turn towards the screen most of the time
explanation: A steady, open posture looks confident and helps your voice carry.

body: Someone asks a question you did not understand. What should you do?
options: Answer something close enough
Politely ask them to repeat or rephrase it
Ignore the question
Say the question is not relevant
explanation: Asking for clarification is professional and leads to a better answer.

body: Your mind goes blank in the middle of your talk. What should you do?
options: Pause, glance at your notes or the current slide, and continue with the next point
Apologise and leave the stage
Start again from the beginning
Fill the gap with made-up details
explanation: A short pause looks natural to the audience. Notes and slides are there to guide you back.

body: The audience looks bored. What is the best response?
options: Speak faster to finish sooner
Ask them to pay attention
Read the slides louder
Ask a quick question or share an example to re-engage them
explanation: Interaction and concrete examples bring attention back quickly.

body: You have 3 minutes but prepared 6 minutes of content. What should you do?
options: Speak twice as fast
Skip the conclusion
Cut down to the two or three most important points and practise again
Ask for more time on stage
explanation: Choosing what matters most respects the time limit and keeps the message clear.

body: During a seminar, someone asks a question you cannot answer. What is the best response?
options: Give a confident guess
Say honestly that you are not sure, and offer to find out and follow up
Change the subject
Say the question is out of scope
explanation: Honesty builds credibility; a confident wrong answer damages it.

body: Your audience includes juniors who are new to the topic. How should you adjust?
options: Explain technical terms simply, with examples
Use the full technical vocabulary to sound expert
Skip the basics, since they can look them up
Speak mainly to the seniors in the room
explanation: Speak to your actual audience. Clear explanations make everyone follow, including experts.

body: How should you use hand gestures?
options: Keep your hands behind your back the whole time
Move your hands constantly to show energy
Point at people in the audience
Use natural gestures that match your words
explanation: Natural gestures add emphasis; constant movement distracts.

body: Your microphone suddenly stops working. What should you do?
options: Stop the talk completely
Complain about the organisers
Stay calm, raise your voice and continue, or pause briefly while it is fixed
Continue at the same volume
explanation: Staying composed keeps the audience with you; technical problems are common.

body: An audience member openly disagrees with your point. What is the best response?
options: Argue until they agree
Acknowledge their view, answer with reasons, and offer to discuss more afterwards
Ignore them and move on
Say they have misunderstood the topic
explanation: A respectful, reasoned reply keeps credibility, and taking it offline protects your time.

body: What usually happens to your speaking speed when you are nervous?
options: It speeds up, so slow down on purpose and pause
It slows down too much
It stays the same
It does not matter
explanation: Nerves often make people rush. Deliberate pauses fix this.

body: Why does a short story help in a talk?
options: Stories make the talk longer
Stories can replace facts
Every talk must have a story
Stories are easier to remember and link the audience to your point
explanation: A relevant story gives a point context and makes it stick.

body: What should a one-minute interview self-introduction include?
options: Your full life story from school
Mostly family details
Your name, education, one or two key skills or projects, and the role you want
Mostly hobbies
explanation: A focused introduction tells the interviewer why you fit the role.

body: Which practice method helps you improve the most?
options: Only think through the talk in your head
Record yourself or practise in front of a friend, then act on the feedback
Practise only on the day of the talk
Avoid practising so it sounds natural
explanation: Seeing or hearing yourself shows habits you cannot notice while speaking.

body: While you present your project, a panel member says: 'This has been done before.' How should you respond?
options: Acknowledge it, then explain what is different in your work or what you learned and improved
Insist your idea is completely original
Agree and move to your last slide
Say the panel member is mistaken
explanation: Calmly showing your contribution turns a challenge into a strength.

body: Your laptop fails two minutes before your slides are due. What should you do?
options: Cancel the presentation
Wait silently until it is fixed
Spend the time apologising
Present the key points from your notes and offer to share the slides later
explanation: Knowing your content well means you can still deliver the message.

body: You have to speak right after a very confident, popular speaker. What helps most?
options: Copy their style
Joke that you cannot match them
Focus on your own message and audience, and start strongly with your planned opening
Cut your talk down to a minute
explanation: Comparing yourself drains confidence. A strong opening resets the room's attention.

body: Someone points out that a number on your slide is wrong. What should you do?
options: Defend the number
Thank them, acknowledge the error, and share the corrected figure afterwards
Ignore the comment
Quietly skip the slide
explanation: Owning a mistake openly protects your credibility more than defending it.

body: You are speaking in a large hall where many listeners are not comfortable with English. How should you adapt?
options: Use simple sentences, a slower pace and visuals, and check understanding
Speak quickly so you cover more
Use advanced vocabulary to sound expert
Drop the visuals and only talk
explanation: Clear, simple delivery helps the whole audience understand you.

body: A panel member asks you a hostile question. What is the best way to handle it?
options: Answer with the same tone
Point out that the question is unfair
Give a short answer and move on quickly
Stay calm, restate the question neutrally, and answer with facts
explanation: Restating neutrally takes the heat out and shows you are composed and fair.

body: You are giving a webinar with everyone's camera off, so you cannot see reactions. What should you do?
options: Talk non-stop until the end
Assume everyone has understood
Ask for questions or reactions in the chat at intervals, or use quick polls
Finish early because no one is responding
explanation: Planned check-ins replace the feedback you would normally see on faces.

body: After your talk, what is the best way to improve for next time?
options: Move on without thinking about it
Ask a few listeners for specific feedback and pick one or two things to change
Judge it only by how many people clapped
Assume any problems were the audience's fault
explanation: Specific feedback plus a small number of focused changes leads to steady improvement.
